sets.title: A tour of the science museum
sets.description: Section 2 — monolog pemandu: denah & pilihan ganda
sets.transcript:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Harbour Science Museum. My name's Tom, and I'll be your guide for the first part of your visit. Before we start, let me give you a quick overview of the building so you can find your way around later.

We're standing in the main hall, right by the ticket desk. If you look straight ahead, you'll see the large staircase. The cloakroom, where you can leave coats and bags free of charge, is on your left, just past the gift shop. Please note that large backpacks are not allowed in the galleries, so do leave them there.

On the ground floor, the most popular area is the Space Gallery, which is through the double doors to the right of the staircase. It has a full-size model of a Mars rover, and children love it. Opposite the Space Gallery, you'll find the café. It serves hot lunches until two o'clock, and after that just snacks and drinks.

Now, the first floor. At the top of the stairs, turn left for the Energy Zone. This is our newest gallery — it only opened last month — and it's very hands-on: you can generate electricity by riding a bike or design your own wind turbine. If you turn right at the top of the stairs instead, you'll reach the Human Body exhibition. I should mention that part of it is closed today for repairs, so the heart and lungs section won't be open, but the rest is.

There's also a planetarium on the second floor. Shows last twenty-five minutes and start every hour. Tickets are not included in your entry ticket — they cost three pounds fifty — and they often sell out, so I'd recommend booking at the information point as soon as possible.

A couple of practical points. Photography is allowed everywhere except in the planetarium. The museum closes at half past five, but the galleries start closing at five fifteen. And if you lose anyone in your group, please go to the information point by the main entrance rather than the ticket desk.

Right, our tour begins in the Space Gallery, so if you'd like to follow me…

sets.title: Planning a presentation on urban heat
sets.description: Section 3 — diskusi akademik dua mahasiswa dan tutor
sets.transcript:
Dr Patel (tutor): So, Maya, Leo — you've chosen urban heat islands for your presentation. How's the planning going?

Maya (student): Pretty well, I think. We've divided it into three parts: causes, effects on health, and solutions.

Leo (student): Although we're still not sure how much time to give each part.

Dr Patel (tutor): What does your research suggest is the most interesting area?

Leo (student): Personally, I thought the causes would be the main focus — dark roads, fewer trees, heat from air conditioners and so on. But when we looked at the data, the solutions part was much richer.

Maya (student): Yes, there are some really creative projects. Cities painting roofs white, planting trees along bus routes…

Dr Patel (tutor): Then I'd suggest giving the solutions about half of your time. The audience will already know the basic causes.

Maya (student): That makes sense. For the health effects, we were going to use a case study from Paris.

Leo (student): We did consider the Chicago heatwave in 1995, but there's so much written about it already.

Dr Patel (tutor): Paris is a good choice, but make sure your figures are recent. Some of the statistics online are more than twenty years old.

Maya (student): Right. We found a government report from 2022, so we'll use that.

Dr Patel (tutor): Good. What about visuals?

Leo (student): I wanted to show a thermal map of the city, where you can see the hot areas in red.

Maya (student): And I'd like to include a short video interview, but Leo thinks it'll take too long.

Leo (student): We only have fifteen minutes in total.

Dr Patel (tutor): I agree with Leo. A video of more than a minute will eat into your time. The thermal map will make the point more quickly.

Maya (student): OK, no video then.

Dr Patel (tutor): And how are you dividing the speaking?

Leo (student): Maya will introduce the topic and present the health effects, and I'll cover causes and solutions.

Dr Patel (tutor): That puts a lot on you, Leo. Why not let Maya present some of the solutions? It'll also make the transition smoother.

Maya (student): I'm happy to do the green roofs part. I actually visited one in Singapore.

Dr Patel (tutor): Perfect — a personal example will make it more memorable. Finally, what's your biggest worry?

Leo (student): Honestly, the questions at the end. We're not experts in climate science.

Dr Patel (tutor): Nobody expects you to be. If you don't know an answer, just say what you would need to find out. That's a perfectly good academic response.

sets.title: Lecture: How honeybees find their way
sets.transcript:
Good afternoon. In today's lecture I want to look at a remarkable skill: how honeybees find their way between the hive and the flowers they feed on, sometimes several kilometres away.

The first and most important tool is the sun. Bees use the position of the sun as a kind of compass. What's surprising is that they can still do this on cloudy days. This is because their eyes can detect polarised light, a pattern in the sky that humans cannot see. So even when the sun itself is hidden, the bee knows where it is.

Of course, the sun moves across the sky during the day, so a fixed compass would not be enough. Bees solve this with an internal clock. Experiments in the nineteen-fifties showed that bees which were trained to visit a feeder in the morning would still fly in the correct direction in the afternoon, adjusting for the sun's movement.

The second tool is distance measurement. For a long time, scientists assumed that bees measured distance by the energy they used. However, research in the year two thousand showed something different. Bees actually measure distance by how much the image of the ground moves across their eyes — what we call optic flow. When researchers made bees fly through a narrow tunnel with a striped pattern on the walls, the bees behaved as if they had flown much further than they really had.

Thirdly, bees use landmarks. Near the hive, they learn the shape of the surroundings — trees, buildings, even the edges of fields. Before a young bee starts collecting food, it makes several orientation flights, circling the hive and memorising what it sees.

Finally, bees share information. A forager that has found a good source of food returns to the hive and performs the famous waggle dance. The angle of the dance tells the other bees the direction relative to the sun, and the length of the waggle part indicates the distance. A longer waggle means the food is further away.

Why does any of this matter beyond biology? Engineers are now using these ideas to design small flying robots. Because optic flow requires very little computing power, it is ideal for drones that need to navigate indoors, where satellite positioning does not work. In the next lecture we'll look at some of these designs in more detail.

sets.title: Mock Part 2: Beach clean-up volunteers
sets.transcript:
Hi everyone, and thanks so much for volunteering for this Saturday's beach clean-up. I'm Grace, and I coordinate the volunteer programme here at Coastcare. I'll explain how the day will run and what you need to bring.

We'll meet at seven thirty in the morning in the car park at the northern end of Bayview Beach, next to the lifeguard tower. Please don't go to the southern car park — it's being resurfaced, and it's closed this weekend.

When you arrive, you'll register with one of our team leaders and receive a pair of gloves, a bucket and a grabber, which is a long stick for picking up rubbish without bending down. We've had a lot of new volunteers this year, so we may run short of grabbers. If you've got your own, please bring it along.

Please wear clothes you don't mind getting dirty, and strong shoes — not sandals, because there can be broken glass in the sand. Bring a hat and plenty of water. We provide sunscreen, so you don't need to pack that.

The beach will be divided into four zones. Families with young children will work in Zone A, close to the playground, where the sand is clean and soft. Zone B is the rocky area, and that's for experienced volunteers only. Zones C and D cover the dunes, and in those zones please stay on the marked paths, as birds are nesting there at this time of year.

Now, what happens to the rubbish? Everything you collect goes to the sorting tent. We separate plastic bottles, fishing equipment and everything else. We then record the numbers on our data sheet, and the results go to a national research project on ocean pollution. Last year, the item we found most often was cigarette ends, followed by plastic bottle caps.

We'll finish at eleven o'clock. After that, there's a free barbecue for all volunteers, kindly provided by a local supermarket. And for anyone who completes five clean-ups this year, we'll give you a certificate, which can be useful if you're applying for jobs in environmental work.

Any questions so far? No? Great — let's look at the safety rules.

sets.title: Mock Part 3: Food waste research project
sets.transcript:
Hana (student): Marcus, have you had a chance to look at the results from the canteen survey?

Marcus (student): Yes, I went through them last night. The headline figure is that about thirty percent of the food served at lunch ends up in the bin.

Hana (student): Thirty? I expected it to be higher, to be honest, given what we saw on the first day.

Marcus (student): The first day was a Monday, and they'd cooked extra because of a staff event that was cancelled. If we take that day out, it's actually twenty-six percent.

Hana (student): Good point. We should mention that in our methodology section, so readers know why we excluded it.

Marcus (student): Agreed. What about the types of food? Vegetables were the most wasted category.

Hana (student): That's not surprising. But I think the more interesting finding is about bread. Students threw away almost half the bread rolls they took.

Marcus (student): Because they're free and placed next to the till, so people just grab one without thinking.

Hana (student): Exactly. So one recommendation could be to move the bread to the start of the counter, or to make students ask for it.

Marcus (student): I like asking for it. It's cheap, and it doesn't need any changes to the layout.

Hana (student): OK. And the second recommendation is about portion sizes. Lots of people said the plates were too full.

Marcus (student): Right, so we could suggest offering a small portion at a lower price.

Hana (student): Although the canteen manager told us they tried that two years ago and almost nobody chose it.

Marcus (student): Because the price difference was tiny. If the small portion was, say, a pound cheaper, I think people would take it.

Hana (student): Maybe. We should present it as something to trial for a term rather than a firm recommendation.

Marcus (student): Fair enough. Now, how do we present the data? I was thinking a pie chart for the food categories.

Hana (student): A pie chart with eight categories would be hard to read. A bar chart would be clearer.

Marcus (student): True. And for the change over the two weeks, a line graph.

Hana (student): Yes. Then we need to decide who writes what. I could do the literature review, since I've already read most of the articles.

Marcus (student): Then I'll take the results and the charts. And we'll write the conclusion together.

Hana (student): Sounds good. The deadline's the twelfth, so let's aim to have a full draft by the fifth.

sets.title: Mock Part 4: Ancient water tunnels
sets.transcript:
Today I'd like to talk about one of the most impressive engineering achievements of the ancient world, and one that is still in use in some places: the qanat, an underground tunnel used to bring water to dry regions.

Qanats were first developed in ancient Persia, in what is now Iran, about three thousand years ago. The idea later spread across the Middle East, North Africa and even to Spain, and from there to parts of South America.

So how does a qanat work? It begins at the foot of a hill or mountain, where water is found underground. Workers dug a vertical shaft, which we call the mother well, down to the level of the groundwater. Then, starting from the village or farmland, they dug a gently sloping tunnel back towards that mother well. The slope had to be very slight. If it was too steep, the water would flow too fast and wear away the tunnel walls.

Along the length of the tunnel, workers dug more vertical shafts at regular intervals. These served two purposes: they allowed the soil to be removed, and they provided fresh air for the diggers. From above, a qanat looks like a long line of small craters across the desert.

The main advantage of a qanat is that the water travels underground, so very little is lost to evaporation, which is a major problem with open canals in hot climates. Also, because gravity moves the water, no pumps or energy are needed.

The workers who built and maintained qanats were highly skilled specialists, and the profession was often passed down from father to son. It was dangerous work; tunnels could collapse, and the workers had to rely on simple tools such as a lamp to check the direction and the quality of the air.

Qanats also shaped the design of buildings. In some Persian houses, cool air from the tunnel was drawn up into the rooms, providing a natural form of air conditioning. Some qanats even supplied underground ice houses, where ice was stored throughout the summer.

Today, many qanats have fallen out of use, mainly because modern electric pumps allow farmers to extract groundwater much faster. Unfortunately, this has lowered the water table, causing some old qanats to dry up. However, there is renewed interest in restoring them, because they offer a sustainable way to manage water. In twenty sixteen, eleven Persian qanats were added to the UNESCO World Heritage List.
